Named from the Argentinean Navy's Submarine A.R.A. "San Juan", lost on November 17th of 2017. The wreck was found at depth of 907 m on this feature on November 18th of 2018.
Named from the nearby Komba Island, northeast of East Nusa Tenggara Province, Indonesia.

Named from the nearby Abrolhos Archipelago. The specific term Abrolhos which means "open eyes; to stare" was used by the ancient Portuguese navigators when arriving in this shallow area with many coral reefs.

Named after the nearby Aby Lagoon.
Named from the nearby Mexican city of Acapulco.
Named from the adjacent feature on land, Cape Adare.
Named after the nearby land feature Cape Adare, which was named after an officer of the Ross expedition in the 1840s.

Named in association with the land feature, Cape Adare, which itself was named by Captain James Ross (1800-1862) for his friend Viscount Adare (1812-1861), Member of Parliament for Glamorganshire, England.
Named after the adjacent Cape Adieu.

In 1969, R.K. Williams, the hydrographer in charge on the CCGS "John A. Macdonald", saw a shoal patch showing up suddenly on the echo sounder. He called Admiral Antony Storrs, of the Ministry of Transport, to take a look. The Admiral rushed over, saying "Where?" and then, "You mean that!" as he poked his finger at the sounder bending the stylus on the machine.
Named after the nearby Admiralteystvo Peninsula. This is the Russian spelling of "Admiralty", which was the former name of the Russian Navy.

Named in association with Admiralty Mountains on the adjacent Victoria Land in Antarctica. The mountains were discovered in 1841 by Capt. James Ross (English Royal Navy) and named by him for the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty under whose orders he served.
Name given by Dutch scientists, AEGIS is the name of a Dutch Research Vessel.

Named after Fyodor Prokop'yevich Afanasenkov (1912-1988), a Russian hydrographer who participated in 38 expeditions in the northern seas of the Arctic Ocean region. He participated in complex oceanographic research conducted by air expeditions in high latitudes.

Named after Afanasij Nikitin, a XVth century Russian traveller who, in 1471-1474, reached the Indian Ocean, moving from Moscow through the Volga River, Caspian and Mediterranean seas, across Persia and Buchara. He wrote a book entitled "Voyaging on the Three Seas".
Named from the South African fisheries research vessel "Africana II" which worked extensively in this area in the 1960s.

Named after Leonid Petrovich Agafonov (1914-1996), a Russian hydrographer who for more than 35 years led and personally participated in hydrographic works in the northern seas of the Novaya Zemlya, Barents and White Seas.

Named after Galina Vladimirovna Agapova (1930-2018), a marine geomorphologist and cartographer at the Russian Academy of Sciences since 1955. She participated in many expeditions in various seas and oceans, relating to the discovery and research of underwater features such as seamounts or ridges. Named from the Agoho tree (Casuarina equisetifolia), a native Philippine tree with oval-shaped fruit. The fruits resemble cones with persistent bracts. The species can be found all over the Philippines, along sandy seashores and inland in broad sandy valleys near streams. It has been observed growing at elevations of up to 800 metres.
Named after the Azores geophysicist José Agostinho, author of many books, mainly on Azores meteorology (1st half of XXth Century). Example: O Clima dos Açores in Açoreana (1930-1940).
Named from the nearby Aguja Island, Colombia.
Named from the nearby Cape Agulhas, in South Africa, the geographic southern tip of the African continent and the beginning of the dividing line between the Atlantic and Indian Oceans.
Named from the nearby Agulhas Ridge. The feature looks like wings, hence the name.

Ahiparaha is a new Māori word for albacore tuna. It is a cognate of the Hawaiian word for albacore tuna ‘ahipalaha’. A licensed translator of te reo Māori has confirmed the orthography for the new word and the appropriateness of adding a new word for albacore tuna to te reo Māori. Aho is the Māori word for a fishing line, and the feature is adjacent to the seamount named Upokororo (a fish).
Named from the Tongan word “Ahohaka” which means “Storm” in that language. The feature lies in the vicinity of Tonga.
Named from the Tongan word “Ahomana” which means “Thunder” in that language.

"Ai Temto" is a Sobey term (Papuan language). "Ai" means 'drifting logs', referring to the drifting logs sometimes found around this location. "Temto" means 'men' as it is believed that behind these logs there are men who bring the blessing of lots of fish.

Named in association with Aiguilles Island on the northern tip of Great Barrier Island (Aotea Island). 'Aiguilles' (the French for 'needles') describes the pointed rocks on the adjacent Needles Point.
L' Aiguillon is a small town located on the Atlantic coast, NW of the city of La Rochelle, on the west coast of France.
Named from the nearby village area of Aipiri, in the northern part of Manokwari, West Papua, Indonesia.

The term "Airawat" originates from Sanskrit language and designates a mythological white elephant with multiple trunks, considered the mount of the god ‘Indra’. According to Hindu mythology, Airawat emerged during the churning of the cosmic ocean (Samudra Manthan) by the gods and demons. Aix is a small island located between the city of La Rochelle and Oleron island, off the western coast of France.
Named from the nearby Aka Island, a major constituent island of the Kerama Islands.
"Akaboshi" is one of the Japanese dialect names that means the Antares Star in the Constellation of Scorpius.
Named from the Russian Academy of Sciences which organized many expeditions to the northern part of the Pacific Ocean from 1949 to 1957.
Named after the Soviet Research Ship "Akademik Fedorov" which worked in this area in 1989.
Named from the Russian R/V "Akademik Kurchatov" that closely investigated this feature.
Named in association with Akaroa Harbour and Akaroa Head, on the adjacent mainland. Lit. aka (whanga): harbour; roa: long.

Named from the Philippine swamphen (Porphyrio pulverulentus), locally known as “akbag,” a bird endemic to Philippine wetlands like those in Pampanga. It represents the country’s fragile wetland ecosystems and contributes to sustaining rice field biodiversity, which is crucial to food security and rural life.
"Myojo" means, in Japanese, Venus seen before sunrise or after sunset.
"Aki-No-Nanakusa" means "the seven flowers of autumn" in Japanese.

Named after the Japanese author, poet, pioneering feminist, pacifist, and social reformer Akiko Yosano (1878-1942), during the late Meiji to early Showa periods of Japan. She was one of the most famous and controversial post-classical woman poets of Japan. Akiko is the first name as, at that time, it was common and popular for Japanese writers to be called by their first names. This feature is par

Named after Dr. Toshio Akiyoshi (1889-1947), a Japanese geophysicist. When astronomical almanacs could not be imported into Japan during World War II, he was in charge of developing an astronomical navigation table, which resulted in Japan's own astronomical navigation table (Japanese ephemeris) in 1943.

"Akki" is a Polynesian-named dolphin character from the novel “Startide Rising” by David Brin, which won the Hugo Award for best science-fiction novel in 1984. The area of the feature is in French Polynesia.

Named from the "Akle", a medium-sized deciduous tree, intolerant to shade, which is found in humid lowland forests of the Philippines. The wood is one of the best materials for cabinetmaking because of its color, good-grain quality, and durability. It is also used for gunstocks, carvings, sculpture, and musical instruments, as well as for interior finish, panels, and high-grade furniture.
Named after Eduard Nikolayevich Akopov (1926-1991), a Russian hydrographer who served in the Pacific Fleet. He conducted hydrographic research in the Sea of Japan, Sea of Okhotsk and Bering Sea.

Named from an old name of the city of Sur, located near the feature, about 150 km southeast of the Oman capital, Muscat. This coastal city was renowned for its trade with East Africa as well as for its long-standing prominence in the shipbuilding industry.

Named from the "Bum", a traditional wooden sailing dhow that appeared in the twentieth century but the history of its use extends to ancient times and the use of the Bum ships for commercial purposes was common across the western side of the Indian Ocean and the Arabian Gulf.
"Al Ghubayra" is one of the ancient names of Oman dating back to the 6th century.

"Al Jurz" is a stick and a part of Omani heritage, famous in Musandam Governorate at the North of Oman. It consists of two parts: a wooden stick and a metal axe, both being made from the local environment. The stick is decorated with geometric engravings, making it a beautiful artwork. Men in Musandam carry "Al Jurz" in traditional ceremonies.

The term "Al Kharif" refers to the unique season in the southern part of Oman that occurs during the period from June to September when the monsoon brings coolness and light rain, and turns the region into a lush green paradise, while most of the Arabian Peninsula witnesses a rise in temperature.

Named from the oldest type of dhow made by the Omanis, locally known as "Al Qitran". It consists of a number of plates of wood stacked on top of each other. This is one of the famous sea-going boats in the Wilayat of Sur. The Arabic term "Al Qitran" means "bitumen", which was used as a coating for ocean-going boats. About 200 well-preserved bitumen slabs and 100 smaller fragments dating from 2,300

Named after Valerian I. Al'banov (1882-1919), Russian navigator on the ship "Svyataya Anna" and leader of the expedition of G. Brusilov (1912-1914) in the Arctic. Al'banov and fourteen sailors left the drifting ship near 83°N-60°E and after three months reached Cape Flora. Al'banov kept documents of the missing ship.

Named from the Alagau, a forest tree with medicinal uses that is endemic to the Philippines. It is commonly found in thickets and secondary forests at low altitudes; sometimes purposely planted around dwellings in most provinces, from Luzon to Mindanao. Decoction of its leaves and flowers is effective for cough, fever, abdominal pain, vaginal irritation, and urination problems

Named from the "Alamang", an Indonesian traditional weapon from South Sulawesi. It is usually used as a weapon for self-defense, and is a symbol of sovereignty, prosperity and royal authority. A king would never leave his kingdom without taking his Alamang.
Named after Texas A&M Research Ship "Alaminos".

Named from the city of Alaminos, in the Philippines province of Pangasinan. Established as a municipality in 1747, Alaminos is known for being the home of the famous Hundred Islands, a national park and protected area, composed of 123 islets scattered throughout the Lingayen Gulf.
Named after the Portuguese Hydrographic Survey ship Albacora (1924-1942).
In recognition of Prince Albert 1er of Monaco's work improving the knowledge of the Azores region.
Named after Francisco Albo, a navigator and member of Magellan's expedition who kept an account of the expedition.

Named after Dr. Angel C. Alcala (1929–2023), a Filipino renowned marine biologist, graduate of Stanford University, USA (MS and Ph.D). He made vast contributions to research in marine biodiversity and conservation. His pioneering work on marine protected areas led to a national policy and program on marine no-take zones, which became a coastal resource management and conservation model adopted by
A. Alcock (UK) made marine studies in the late 1800s. Author of "A Naturalist in Indian Seas", London, 1902.
Named in association with The Aldermen Islands, which were named by Capt. Cook in 1769 after the 'Court of Aldermen', an elected body that formed part of the City of London Corporation.
Named from the nearby Aleutian Islands.
Named by John Ross in 1818, after the "Alexander", one of the vessels he commanded.

Named after Alexander Agassiz (1835-1910), a Swiss-born American marine zoologist, oceanographer, and mining engineer who made important contributions to systematic zoology, to the knowledge of ocean beds, and to the development of a major copper mine. In 1875 he surveyed Lake Titicaca, Peru, and made a collection of Peruvian antiquities for the Museum of Comparative Zoology, of which he was curat

Named from the "Algerine" , a Newfoundland ship owned by Bowring Brothers of St. John's. She was chartered by the White Star Line late in the search, to operate with the Canadian government vessel "Montmagny". She left St. John's on May 15, 1912, and returned June 8, 1912. She recovered the last body, that of James McGrady, who was buried in Halifax.
Named from the nearby Alice Shoal.

Na-ed after Alix de Chazal Baissac, wife/colleague of 40-year Mauritius Fishery Officer-naturalist Jean De Baissac for whom Baissac Bank is named. For 5O years, the pair welcomed and provided significant aid to marine scientists who visited or did field work in the Mascarene region.
Named after Mike H. Allen (1948-1978), HIG researcher lost at sea when the vessel "Holoholo" was lost during an oceanographic voyage.

Named from the Almaciga tree (Agathis philippinensis), a tree native to the Philippines. Almaciga is prized for its high-grade resin, known as Manila copal. The tapping of this resin is the primary livelihood for many indigenous people in Sierra Madre mountain range and Palawan forests.
Named from the Portuguese Hydrographic survey vessel "Almeida Carvalho".

Named from the Brazilian research vessel "Almirante Câmara" that discovered this feature and conducted many surveys on the Brazilian continental Margin from 1975. Almirante Antonio Alves Câmara Junior was one of the most important persons involved in the establishment of the Brazilian Hydrographic Service.

Named from the Brazilian Navy oceanographic vessel "Almirante Câmara" that discovered this feature. The vessel name is a tribute to Admiral Antônio Alves Câmara Júnior (1891-1958), who was an important promoter of Brazilian hydrography.

Named from the blue subgiant star "Alpha Crucis", located in the South Cross constellation (Cruzeiro do Sul, in Portuguese) in the southern hemisphere, in association with the nearby Cruzeiro do Sul Rift. Alpha Crucis is the main and southern most star of the South Cross constellation and marks the bottom of the South Cross, when facing south.
Named from the research vessel "Altair" of the Russian Fisheries Ministry that worked in the area of this feature.
Named after Friedrich Althoff (1839-1909), German lawyer and patron of the 1899 Valdivia Expedition led by Carl Chun.
Named from the adjacent Althorpe Islands, South Australia.
Named from its location as this feature extends from the Ras Alula, Somalia to the Ras Fartak, Yemen.

Named after “Alunsina”, a prominent deity revered as the goddess of the eastern skies in the Panay pantheon. Her divine presence was believed to usher in the sun's radiance and refreshing breezes during the dry season's scorching days. She was also venerated for safeguarding against powerful typhoons and was linked to concepts of elegance, matrimony, and femininity. "Alunsina" was regarded as the

Named from the Alupag tree, an evergreen fruit-bearing plant indigenous to the Philippines. This tree is a close relative of litchi and produces delicious fruits. It can grow up to 7-10 meters tall and has leathery textured leaves that can reach up to 30 cm in length with 6-9 pairs of leaflets. Alupag thrives in places with a subtropical climate or tropical highlands and can be propagated by seed,
Name of one of the first inhabitants of Azores Central Islands (Terceira).

Named from the geological cruise Amadeus which took place in 2005, where bathymetric surveying, reflexion seismic and refraction seismic were carried out, in the area of North of Ecuador and South of Colombia. From this campaign and from sismogenetic sources, there have been explanations on the process of subduction in Ecuador.
Named from the adjacent Amami Oshima Island, Japan.
Named from the nearby Amami Island, Japan.
Named after the nearby Amami Oshima Island, Japan ("Sankaku" means "triangle" in Japanese).

Named after "Aman Sinaya", the sea deity invoked by early Filipino fishers, who symbolizes the intimate link between myth and livelihood. His name preserves the legacy of maritime traditions and ocean reverence.
Named from the nearby Amazon State, Brazil, and Amazon River.
Named from its shape as this feature looks like a horn of a sea hare, "Amefurashi" in Japanese.
Named after the Argentinean scientist Florentino Ameghino.

In the local Sobey language (Papua), "Amfiro" means "Undersea princess" . Local communities previously believed that a princess once lived at that location, who later died and her carcass floated to form an undersea escarpment.
Named from the nearby Amirante Islands, Seychelles.
Named from the nearby Amirante Islands, Seychelles.
Named from the nearby Amlia Island, in the Aleutian Islands, Alaska, USA.

Named after Daniel Ammen (1820-1898), a Rear Admiral in the U.S. Navy. He served in coast survey duty for the Navy. Later, he served as the chief of the Bureau of Navigation (1871-1878), which enforced laws relating to the construction, equipment, operation, inspection, safety, and documentation of merchant vessels. Named from the nearby Amphitheatre Escarpment.
Named from its shape as this feature resembles 2 amphitheatres side by side.

Named from the "Amugis", a large evergreen tree, which is endemic to the Philippines especially in the Luzon provinces. It is widely used for flooring, general construction, and various medicinal purposes.
Named from the nearby Amukta Island, in the Aleutian Islands, Alaska, USA.

Named after the Norwegian Polar explorer Roald Amundsen 1872-1928, who led the expedition that first reached the South Pole in 1911. He also was the first to fly over the North Pole on an airship in 1926.

Named after the Norvegian Polar explorer Roald Amundsen 1872-1928, who led the expedition that first reached the South Pole in 1911. He also was the first to fly over the North Pole on a airship in 1926.

Named from the locality of An Ngãi, district of Long Dien, province of Ba Ria – Vung Tau, Viet Nam.
Name after the locality of An Phú, city of Tuy Hoa, province of Phu Yen, Viet Nam.

Named from the locality of An Thủy, district of Ba Tri, province of Ben Tre, Viet Nam.
Named from the Japanese era “An-ei” (1722-1781) in the Edo Period.
Named in association with the nearby An-ei Seamount, which itself was named from the Japanese era “An-ei” (1722-1781) in the Edo Period.
Named in association with Batutara Island which is located 58 km to the southeast of the feature, in the Flores Sea, Indonesia. "anak" means 'child' in Indonesian language.
"Anakena" is the name of a beach on Easter Island where the first settlers landed.
Named from Anakena Beach, on the nearby Easter Island, Chile, where the first settlers landed.
The term ‘Anant’ means "Endless" or "Infinite" in Sanskrit, symbolizing the boundless expanse of the ocean.

Named after Dr. Toshio Akiyoshi (1889-1947), a Japanese geophysicist. When astronomical almanacs could not be imported into Japan during World War II, he was in charge of developing an astronomical navigation table, which resulted in Japan's own astronomical navigation table (Japanese ephemeris) in 1943.

"Akki" is a Polynesian-named dolphin character from the novel “Startide Rising” by David Brin, which won the Hugo Award for best science-fiction novel in 1984. The area of the feature is in French Polynesia.

Named from the "Akle", a medium-sized deciduous tree, intolerant to shade, which is found in humid lowland forests of the Philippines. The wood is one of the best materials for cabinetmaking because of its color, good-grain quality, and durability. It is also used for gunstocks, carvings, sculpture, and musical instruments, as well as for interior finish, panels, and high-grade furniture.
Named after Eduard Nikolayevich Akopov (1926-1991), a Russian hydrographer who served in the Pacific Fleet. He conducted hydrographic research in the Sea of Japan, Sea of Okhotsk and Bering Sea.

Named from an old name of the city of Sur, located near the feature, about 150 km southeast of the Oman capital, Muscat. This coastal city was renowned for its trade with East Africa as well as for its long-standing prominence in the shipbuilding industry.

Named from the "Bum", a traditional wooden sailing dhow that appeared in the twentieth century but the history of its use extends to ancient times and the use of the Bum ships for commercial purposes was common across the western side of the Indian Ocean and the Arabian Gulf.
"Al Ghubayra" is one of the ancient names of Oman dating back to the 6th century.

"Al Jurz" is a stick and a part of Omani heritage, famous in Musandam Governorate at the North of Oman. It consists of two parts: a wooden stick and a metal axe, both being made from the local environment. The stick is decorated with geometric engravings, making it a beautiful artwork. Men in Musandam carry "Al Jurz" in traditional ceremonies.

The term "Al Kharif" refers to the unique season in the southern part of Oman that occurs during the period from June to September when the monsoon brings coolness and light rain, and turns the region into a lush green paradise, while most of the Arabian Peninsula witnesses a rise in temperature.

Named from the oldest type of dhow made by the Omanis, locally known as "Al Qitran". It consists of a number of plates of wood stacked on top of each other. Al'banov and fourteen sailors left the drifting ship near 83°N-60°E and after three months reached Cape Flora. Al'banov kept documents of the missing ship.

Named from the first Omani ship "Sultanah" that sailed in 1840 on a historic voyage from Zanzibar to the USA. Named from the nearby Komba Island, northeast of East Nusa Tenggara Province, Indonesia.

Named from the nearby Abrolhos Archipelago. The specific term Abrolhos which means "open eyes; to stare" was used by the ancient Portuguese navigators when arriving in this shallow area with many coral reefs.

Named after the adjacent Cape Adieu.

In 1969, R.K. Williams, the hydrographer in charge on the CCGS "John A. Macdonald", saw a shoal patch showing up suddenly on the echo sounder. He called Admiral Antony Storrs, of the Ministry of Transport, to take a look. The Admiral rushed over, saying "Where?" and then, "You mean that!" as he poked his finger at the sounder bending the stylus on the machine.
Named after the nearby Admiralteystvo Peninsula. This is the Russian spelling of "Admiralty", which was the former name of the Russian Navy.

Named in association with Admiralty Mountains on the adjacent Victoria Land in Antarctica. The mountains were discovered in 1841 by Capt. James Ross (English Royal Navy) and named by him for the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty under whose orders he served.

Named after Fyodor Prokop'yevich Afanasenkov (1912-1988), a Russian hydrographer who participated in 38 expeditions in the northern seas of the Arctic Ocean region. He participated in complex oceanographic research conducted by air expeditions in high latitudes.

Named after Afanasij Nikitin, a XVth century Russian traveller who, in 1471-1474, reached the Indian Ocean, moving from Moscow through the Volga River, Caspian and Mediterranean seas, across Persia and Buchara. He wrote a book entitled "Voyaging on the Three Seas".
Named from the South African fisheries research vessel "Africana II" which worked extensively in this area in the 1960s.

Named after Leonid Petrovich Agafonov (1914-1996), a Russian hydrographer who for more than 35 years led and personally participated in hydrographic works in the northern seas of the Novaya Zemlya, Barents and White Seas.

Named after Galina Vladimirovna Agapova (1930-2018), a marine geomorphologist and cartographer at the Russian Academy of Sciences since 1955. The species can be found all over the Philippines, along sandy seashores and inland in broad sandy valleys near streams. It has been observed growing at elevations of up to 800 metres.

Named from the nearby Cape Agulhas, in South Africa, the geographic southern tip of the African continent and the beginning of the dividing line between the Atlantic and Indian Oceans.

Men in Musandam carry "Al Jurz" in traditional ceremonies.

It consists of two parts: a wooden stick and a metal axe, both being made from the local environment. The stick is decorated with geometric engravings, making it a beautiful artwork. Men in Musandam carry "Al Jurz" in traditional ceremonies.

The Admiral rushed over, saying "Where?" and then, "You mean that!" as he poked his finger at the sounder bending the stylus on the machine.

Named from the nearby village area of Aipiri, in the northern part of Manokwari, West Papua, Indonesia.

It represents the country’s fragile wetland ecosystems and contributes to sustaining rice field biodiversity, which is crucial to food security and rural life.
"Myojo" means, in Japanese, Venus seen before sunrise or after sunset.
"Aki-No-Nanakusa" means "the seven flowers of autumn" in Japanese.

Named after the Japanese author, poet, pioneering feminist, pacifist, and social reformer Akiko Yosano (1878-1942), during the late Meiji to early Showa periods of Japan. Named after Dr. Toshio Akiyoshi (1889-1947), a Japanese geophysicist. When astronomical almanacs could not be imported into Japan during World War II, he was in charge of developing an astronomical navigation table, which resulted in Japan's own astronomical navigation table (Japanese ephemeris) in 1943.

"Akki" is a Polynesian-named dolphin character from the novel “Startide Rising” by David Brin, which won the Hugo Award for best science-fiction novel in 1984. The area of the feature is in French Polynesia.

Named from the "Akle", a medium-sized deciduous tree, intolerant to shade, which is found in humid lowland forests of the Philippines. The wood is one of the best materials for cabinetmaking because of its color, good-grain quality, and durability. It is also used for gunstocks, carvings, sculpture, and musical instruments, as well as for interior finish, panels, and high-grade furniture.
Named after Eduard Nikolayevich Akopov (1926-1991), a Russian hydrographer who served in the Pacific Fleet. He conducted hydrographic research in the Sea of Japan, Sea of Okhotsk and Bering Sea.

Named from an old name of the city of Sur, located near the feature, about 150 km southeast of the Oman capital, Muscat. This coastal city was renowned for its trade with East Africa as well as for its long-standing prominence in the shipbuilding industry.

Named from the "Bum", a traditional wooden sailing dhow that appeared in the twentieth century but the history of its use extends to ancient times and the use of the Bum ships for commercial purposes was common across the western side of the Indian Ocean and the Arabian Gulf.
"Al Ghubayra" is one of the ancient names of Oman dating back to the 6th century.

"Al Jurz" is a stick and a part of Omani heritage, famous in Musandam Governorate at the North of Oman. It consists of two parts: a wooden stick and a metal axe, both being made from the local environment. The stick is decorated with geometric engravings, making it a beautiful artwork. Men in Musandam carry "Al Jurz" in traditional ceremonies.

The term "Al Kharif" refers to the unique season in the southern part of Oman that occurs during the period from June to September when the monsoon brings coolness and light rain, and turns the region into a lush green paradise, while most of the Arabian Peninsula witnesses a rise in temperature.

Named from the oldest type of dhow made by the Omanis, locally known as "Al Qitran". It consists of a number of plates of wood stacked on top of each other. Al'banov and fourteen sailors left the drifting ship near 83°N-60°E and after three months reached Cape Flora. Al'banov kept documents of the missing ship.

In 1969, R.K. Williams, the hydrographer in charge on the CCGS "John A. Macdonald", saw a shoal patch showing up suddenly on the echo sounder. The Admiral rushed over, saying "Where?" and then, "You mean that!" as he poked his finger at the sounder bending the stylus on the machine.

Named after Dr. Toshio Akiyoshi (1889-1947), a Japanese geophysicist. When astronomical almanacs could not be imported into Japan during World War II, he was in charge of developing an astronomical navigation table, which resulted in Japan's own astronomical navigation table (Japanese ephemeris) in 1943.

"Akki" is a Polynesian-named dolphin character from the novel “Startide Rising” by David Brin, which won the Hugo Award for best science-fiction novel in 1984. The area of the feature is in French Polynesia.

Named from the "Akle", a medium-sized deciduous tree, intolerant to shade, which is found in humid lowland forests of the Philippines. The wood is one of the best materials for cabinetmaking because of its color, good-grain quality, and durability. It is also used for gunstocks, carvings, sculpture, and musical instruments, as well as for interior finish, panels, and high-grade furniture.
Named after Eduard Nikolayevich Akopov (1926-1991), a Russian hydrographer who served in the Pacific Fleet. He conducted hydrographic research in the Sea of Japan, Sea of Okhotsk and Bering Sea.

Named from an old name of the city of Sur, located near the feature, about 150 km southeast of the Oman capital, Muscat. This coastal city was renowned for its trade with East Africa as well as for its long-standing prominence in the shipbuilding industry.

Named from the "Bum", a traditional wooden sailing dhow that appeared in the twentieth century but the history of its use extends to ancient times and the use of the Bum ships for commercial purposes was common across the western side of the Indian Ocean and the Arabian Gulf.
"Al Ghubayra" is one of the ancient names of Oman dating back to the 6th century.

"Al Jurz" is a stick and a part of Omani heritage, famous in Musandam Governorate at the North of Oman. It consists of two parts: a wooden stick and a metal axe, both being made from the local environment. The stick is decorated with geometric engravings, making it a beautiful artwork. Men in Musandam carry "Al Jurz" in traditional ceremonies.

The term "Al Kharif" refers to the unique season in the southern part of Oman that occurs during the period from June to September when the monsoon brings coolness and light rain, and turns the region into a lush green paradise, while most of the Arabian Peninsula witnesses a rise in temperature.

Named from the oldest type of dhow made by the Omanis, locally known as "Al Qitran". It consists of a number of plates of wood stacked on top of each other. This is one of the famous sea-going boats in the Wilayat of Sur. The Arabic term "Al Qitran" means "bitumen", which was used as a coating for ocean-going boats. Named after Valerian I. Al'banov (1882-1919), Russian navigator on the ship "Svyataya Anna" and leader of the expedition of G. Brusilov (1912-1914) in the Arctic. Al'banov and fourteen sailors left the drifting ship near 83°N-60°E and after three months reached Cape Flora. Al'banov kept documents of the missing ship.

Named from the Alagau, a forest tree with medicinal uses that is endemic to the Philippines. It is commonly found in thickets and secondary forests at low altitudes; sometimes purposely planted around dwellings in most provinces, from Luzon to Mindanao. Decoction of its leaves and flowers is effective for cough, fever, abdominal pain, vaginal irritation, and urination problems

Named from the "Alamang", an Indonesian traditional weapon from South Sulawesi. It is usually used as a weapon for self-defense, and is a symbol of sovereignty, prosperity and royal authority. A king would never leave his kingdom without taking his Alamang.
Named after Texas A&M Research Ship "Alaminos".

Named from the city of Alaminos, in the Philippines province of Pangasinan. Established as a municipality in 1747, Alaminos is known for being the home of the famous Hundred Islands, a national park and protected area, composed of 123 islets scattered throughout the Lingayen Gulf.
Named after the Portuguese Hydrographic Survey ship Albacora (1924-1942).
In recognition of Prince Albert 1er of Monaco's work improving the knowledge of the Azores region.
Named after Francisco Albo, a navigator and member of Magellan's expedition who kept an account of the expedition.

Named after Dr. Angel C. Alcala (1929–2023), a Filipino renowned marine biologist, graduate of Stanford University, USA (MS and Ph.D). He made vast contributions to research in marine biodiversity and conservation. A. Alcock (UK) made marine studies in the late 1800s. Author of "A Naturalist in Indian Seas", London, 1902.
Named in association with The Aldermen Islands, which were named by Capt. Cook in 1769 after the 'Court of Aldermen', an elected body that formed part of the City of London Corporation.
Named from the nearby Aleutian Islands.
Named by John Ross in 1818, after the "Alexander", one of the vessels he commanded.

Named after Alexander Agassiz (1835-1910), a Swiss-born American marine zoologist, oceanographer, and mining engineer who made important contributions to systematic zoology, to the knowledge of ocean beds, and to the development of a major copper mine. Named from the "Algerine" , a Newfoundland ship owned by Bowring Brothers of St. John's. She was chartered by the White Star Line late in the search, to operate with the Canadian government vessel "Montmagny". She left St. John's on May 15, 1912, and returned June 8, 1912. She recovered the last body, that of James McGrady, who was buried in Halifax.
Named from the nearby Alice Shoal.

Na-ed after Alix de Chazal Baissac, wife/colleague of 40-year Mauritius Fishery Officer-naturalist Jean De Baissac for whom Baissac Bank is named. For 5O years, the pair welcomed and provided significant aid to marine scientists who visited or did field work in the Mascarene region.
Named after Mike H. Allen (1948-1978), HIG researcher lost at sea when the vessel "Holoholo" was lost during an oceanographic voyage.

Named from the Almaciga tree (Agathis philippinensis), a tree native to the Philippines. Almaciga is prized for its high-grade resin, known as Manila copal. The tapping of this resin is the primary livelihood for many indigenous people in Sierra Madre mountain range and Palawan forests.
Named from the Portuguese Hydrographic survey vessel "Almeida Carvalho".

Named from the Brazilian research vessel "Almirante Câmara" that discovered this feature and conducted many surveys on the Brazilian continental Margin from 1975. Almirante Antonio Alves Câmara Junior was one of the most important persons involved in the establishment of the Brazilian Hydrographic Service.

Named from the Brazilian Navy oceanographic vessel "Almirante Câmara" that discovered this feature. The vessel name is a tribute to Admiral Antônio Alves Câmara Júnior (1891-1958), who was an important promoter of Brazilian hydrography.

Named from the blue subgiant star "Alpha Crucis", located in the South Cross constellation (Cruzeiro do Sul, in Portuguese) in the southern hemisphere, in association with the nearby Cruzeiro do Sul Rift. Alpha Crucis is the main and southern most star of the South Cross constellation and marks the bottom of the South Cross, when facing south.
Named from the research vessel "Altair" of the Russian Fisheries Ministry that worked in the area of this feature.
Named after Friedrich Althoff (1839-1909), German lawyer and patron of the 1899 Valdivia Expedition led by Carl Chun.
Named from the adjacent Althorpe Islands, South Australia.
Named from its location as this feature extends from the Ras Alula, Somalia to the Ras Fartak, Yemen.

Named after "Aman Sinaya", the sea deity invoked by early Filipino fishers, who symbolizes the intimate link between myth and livelihood. His name preserves the legacy of maritime traditions and ocean reverence.
Named from the nearby Amazon State, Brazil, and Amazon River.
Named from its shape as this feature looks like a horn of a sea hare, "Amefurashi" in Japanese.
Named after the Argentinean scientist Florentino Ameghino.

The wood is one of the best materials for cabinetmaking because of its color, good-grain quality, and durability. It is also used for gunstocks, carvings, sculpture, and musical instruments, as well as for interior finish, panels, and high-grade furniture.
Named after Eduard Nikolayevich Akopov (1926-1991), a Russian hydrographer who served in the Pacific Fleet. He conducted hydrographic research in the Sea of Japan, Sea of Okhotsk and Bering Sea.

Named from an old name of the city of Sur, located near the feature, about 150 km southeast of the Oman capital, Muscat. This coastal city was renowned for its trade with East Africa as well as for its long-standing prominence in the shipbuilding industry.

Named from the "Bum", a traditional wooden sailing dhow that appeared in the twentieth century but the history of its use extends to ancient times and the use of the Bum ships for commercial purposes was common across the western side of the Indian Ocean and the Arabian Gulf.
"Al Ghubayra" is one of the ancient names of Oman dating back to the 6th century.

"Al Jurz" is a stick and a part of Omani heritage, famous in Musandam Governorate at the North of Oman. It consists of two parts: a wooden stick and a metal axe, both being made from the local environment. The stick is decorated with geometric engravings, making it a beautiful artwork. Men in Musandam carry "Al Jurz" in traditional ceremonies.

The term "Al Kharif" refers to the unique season in the southern part of Oman that occurs during the period from June to September when the monsoon brings coolness and light rain, and turns the region into a lush green paradise, while most of the Arabian Peninsula witnesses a rise in temperature.

Named from the oldest type of dhow made by the Omanis, locally known as "Al Qitran". It consists of a number of plates of wood stacked on top of each other. Al'banov and fourteen sailors left the drifting ship near 83°N-60°E and after three months reached Cape Flora. Al'banov kept documents of the missing ship.

In 1969, R.K. Williams, the hydrographer in charge on the CCGS "John A. Macdonald", saw a shoal patch showing up suddenly on the echo sounder. He called Admiral Antony Storrs, of the Ministry of Transport, to take a look. The Admiral rushed over, saying "Where?" and then, "You mean that!" as he poked his finger at the sounder bending the stylus on the machine.
Named after the nearby Admiralteystvo Peninsula. This is the Russian spelling of "Admiralty", which was the former name of the Russian Navy.

Named in association with Admiralty Mountains on the adjacent Victoria Land in Antarctica. The mountains were discovered in 1841 by Capt. James Ross (English Royal Navy) and named by him for the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty under whose orders he served.
Name given by Dutch scientists, AEGIS is the name of a Dutch Research Vessel.

Named after Fyodor Prokop'yevich Afanasenkov (1912-1988), a Russian hydrographer who participated in 38 expeditions in the northern seas of the Arctic Ocean region. He participated in complex oceanographic research conducted by air expeditions in high latitudes.

Named after Afanasij Nikitin, a XVth century Russian traveller who, in 1471-1474, reached the Indian Ocean, moving from Moscow through the Volga River, Caspian and Mediterranean seas, across Persia and Buchara. He wrote a book entitled "Voyaging on the Three Seas".
Named from the South African fisheries research vessel "Africana II" which worked extensively in this area in the 1960s.

Named after Leonid Petrovich Agafonov (1914-1996), a Russian hydrographer who for more than 35 years led and personally participated in hydrographic works in the northern seas of the Novaya Zemlya, Barents and White Seas.

Named after Galina Vladimirovna Agapova (1930-2018), a marine geomorphologist and cartographer at the Russian Academy of Sciences since 1955. The species can be found all over the Philippines, along sandy seashores and inland in broad sandy valleys near streams. It has been observed growing at elevations of up to 800 metres.

"Al Jurz" is a stick and a part of Omani heritage, famous in Musandam Governorate at the North of Oman. It consists of two parts: a wooden stick and a metal axe, both being made from the local environment. The stick is decorated with geometric engravings, making it a beautiful artwork. Men in Musandam carry "Al Jurz" in traditional ceremonies.

The term "Al Kharif" refers to the unique season in the southern part of Oman that occurs during the period from June to September when the monsoon brings coolness and light rain, and turns the region into a lush green paradise, while most of the Arabian Peninsula witnesses a rise in temperature.

Al'banov and fourteen sailors left the drifting ship near 83°N-60°E and after three months reached Cape Flora. Al'banov kept documents of the missing ship.

It consists of two parts: a wooden stick and a metal axe, both being made from the local environment. The stick is decorated with geometric engravings, making it a beautiful artwork. Men in Musandam carry "Al Jurz" in traditional ceremonies.

The term "Al Kharif" refers to the unique season in the southern part of Oman that occurs during the period from June to September when the monsoon brings coolness and light rain, and turns the region into a lush green paradise, while most of the Arabian Peninsula witnesses a rise in temperature.

The Admiral rushed over, saying "Where?" and then, "You mean that!" as he poked his finger at the sounder bending the stylus on the machine.

The wood is one of the best materials for cabinetmaking because of its color, good-grain quality, and durability. It is also used for gunstocks, carvings, sculpture, and musical instruments, as well as for interior finish, panels, and high-grade furniture.

Named from an old name of the city of Sur, located near the feature, about 150 km southeast of the Oman capital, Muscat. This coastal city was renowned for its trade with East Africa as well as for its long-standing prominence in the shipbuilding industry.

Named from the "Bum", a traditional wooden sailing dhow that appeared in the twentieth century but the history of its use extends to ancient times and the use of the Bum ships for commercial purposes was common across the western side of the Indian Ocean and the Arabian Gulf.
"Al Ghubayra" is one of the ancient names of Oman dating back to the 6th century.

"Al Jurz" is a stick and a part of Omani heritage, famous in Musandam Governorate at the North of Oman. It consists of two parts: a wooden stick and a metal axe, both being made from the local environment. The stick is decorated with geometric engravings, making it a beautiful artwork. Men in Musandam carry "Al Jurz" in traditional ceremonies.

The term "Al Kharif" refers to the unique season in the southern part of Oman that occurs during the period from June to September when the monsoon brings coolness and light rain, and turns the region into a lush green paradise, while most of the Arabian Peninsula witnesses a rise in temperature.

Named from the oldest type of dhow made by the Omanis, locally known as "Al Qitran". It consists of a number of plates of wood stacked on top of each other. This is one of the famous sea-going boats in the Wilayat of Sur. The Arabic term "Al Qitran" means "bitumen", which was used as a coating for ocean-going boats. Named after Valerian I. Al'banov (1882-1919), Russian navigator on the ship "Svyataya Anna" and leader of the expedition of G. Brusilov (1912-1914) in the Arctic. Al'banov and fourteen sailors left the drifting ship near 83°N-60°E and after three months reached Cape Flora. Al'banov kept documents of the missing ship.

Named from the Alagau, a forest tree with medicinal uses that is endemic to the Philippines. It is commonly found in thickets and secondary forests at low altitudes; sometimes purposely planted around dwellings in most provinces, from Luzon to Mindanao. Named from the "Alamang", an Indonesian traditional weapon from South Sulawesi. It is usually used as a weapon for self-defense, and is a symbol of sovereignty, prosperity and royal authority. A king would never leave his kingdom without taking his Alamang.
Named after Texas A&M Research Ship "Alaminos".

Named from the city of Alaminos, in the Philippines province of Pangasinan. Established as a municipality in 1747, Alaminos is known for being the home of the famous Hundred Islands, a national park and protected area, composed of 123 islets scattered throughout the Lingayen Gulf.
Named after the Portuguese Hydrographic Survey ship Albacora (1924-1942).
In recognition of Prince Albert 1er of Monaco's work improving the knowledge of the Azores region.
Named after Francisco Albo, a navigator and member of Magellan's expedition who kept an account of the expedition.

Named in association with The Aldermen Islands, which were named by Capt. Cook in 1769 after the 'Court of Aldermen', an elected body that formed part of the City of London Corporation.

Named by John Ross in 1818, after the "Alexander", one of the vessels he commanded.

Named from the "Algerine" , a Newfoundland ship owned by Bowring Brothers of St. John's. She was chartered by the White Star Line late in the search, to operate with the Canadian government vessel "Montmagny". She left St. John's on May 15, 1912, and returned June 8, 1912. She recovered the last body, that of James McGrady, who was buried in Halifax.
Named from the nearby Alice Shoal.

Na-ed after Alix de Chazal Baissac, wife/colleague of 40-year Mauritius Fishery Officer-naturalist Jean De Baissac for whom Baissac Bank is named. For 5O years, the pair welcomed and provided significant aid to marine scientists who visited or did field work in the Mascarene region.
Named after Mike H. Allen (1948-1978), HIG researcher lost at sea when the vessel "Holoholo" was lost during an oceanographic voyage.

Named from the Almaciga tree (Agathis philippinensis), a tree native to the Philippines. Almaciga is prized for its high-grade resin, known as Manila copal. The tapping of this resin is the primary livelihood for many indigenous people in Sierra Madre mountain range and Palawan forests.
Named from the Portuguese Hydrographic survey vessel "Almeida Carvalho".

Named from the Brazilian research vessel "Almirante Câmara" that discovered this feature and conducted many surveys on the Brazilian continental Margin from 1975. Almirante Antonio Alves Câmara Junior was one of the most important persons involved in the establishment of the Brazilian Hydrographic Service.

Named from the Brazilian Navy oceanographic vessel "Almirante Câmara" that discovered this feature. The vessel name is a tribute to Admiral Antônio Alves Câmara Júnior (1891-1958), who was an important promoter of Brazilian hydrography.

Named from the blue subgiant star "Alpha Crucis", located in the South Cross constellation (Cruzeiro do Sul, in Portuguese) in the southern hemisphere, in association with the nearby Cruzeiro do Sul Rift. Alpha Crucis is the main and southern most star of the South Cross constellation and marks the bottom of the South Cross, when facing south.
Named from the research vessel "Altair" of the Russian Fisheries Ministry that worked in the area of this feature.
Named after Friedrich Althoff (1839-1909), German lawyer and patron of the 1899 Valdivia Expedition led by Carl Chun.

Named from the "Bum", a traditional wooden sailing dhow that appeared in the twentieth century but the history of its use extends to ancient times and the use of the Bum ships for commercial purposes was common across the western side of the Indian Ocean and the Arabian Gulf.

"Al Jurz" is a stick and a part of Omani heritage, famous in Musandam Governorate at the North of Oman. It consists of two parts: a wooden stick and a metal axe, both being made from the local environment. The stick is decorated with geometric engravings, making it a beautiful artwork. Men in Musandam carry "Al Jurz" in traditional ceremonies.

The term "Al Kharif" refers to the unique season in the southern part of Oman that occurs during the period from June to September when the monsoon brings coolness and light rain, and turns the region into a lush green paradise, while most of the Arabian Peninsula witnesses a rise in temperature.

Al'banov and fourteen sailors left the drifting ship near 83°N-60°E and after three months reached Cape Flora. Al'banov kept documents of the missing ship.

Men in Musandam carry "Al Jurz" in traditional ceremonies.

The Admiral rushed over, saying "Where?" and then, "You mean that!" as he poked his finger at the sounder bending the stylus on the machine.
Named after the nearby Admiralteystvo Peninsula. This is the Russian spelling of "Admiralty", which was the former name of the Russian Navy.

The wood is one of the best materials for cabinetmaking because of its color, good-grain quality, and durability. Named from an old name of the city of Sur, located near the feature, about 150 km southeast of the Oman capital, Muscat. This coastal city was renowned for its trade with East Africa as well as for its long-standing prominence in the shipbuilding industry.

Named from the "Bum", a traditional wooden sailing dhow that appeared in the twentieth century but the history of its use extends to ancient times and the use of the Bum ships for commercial purposes was common across the western side of the Indian Ocean and the Arabian Gulf.
"Al Ghubayra" is one of the ancient names of Oman dating back to the 6th century.

"Al Jurz" is a stick and a part of Omani heritage, famous in Musandam Governorate at the North of Oman. It consists of two parts: a wooden stick and a metal axe, both being made from the local environment. The stick is decorated with geometric engravings, making it a beautiful artwork. Men in Musandam carry "Al Jurz" in traditional ceremonies.

The term "Al Kharif" refers to the unique season in the southern part of Oman that occurs during the period from June to September when the monsoon brings coolness and light rain, and turns the region into a lush green paradise, while most of the Arabian Peninsula witnesses a rise in temperature.

Named from the oldest type of dhow made by the Omanis, locally known as "Al Qitran". It consists of a number of plates of wood stacked on top of each other. This is one of the famous sea-going boats in the Wilayat of Sur. The Arabic term "Al Qitran" means "bitumen", which was used as a coating for ocean-going boats. Named after Valerian I. Al'banov (1882-1919), Russian navigator on the ship "Svyataya Anna" and leader of the expedition of G. Brusilov (1912-1914) in the Arctic. Al'banov and fourteen sailors left the drifting ship near 83°N-60°E and after three months reached Cape Flora. Al'banov kept documents of the missing ship.

Named from the Alagau, a forest tree with medicinal uses that is endemic to the Philippines. It is commonly found in thickets and secondary forests at low altitudes; sometimes purposely planted around dwellings in most provinces, from Luzon to Mindanao. Named from the "Alamang", an Indonesian traditional weapon from South Sulawesi. It is usually used as a weapon for self-defense, and is a symbol of sovereignty, prosperity and royal authority. A king would never leave his kingdom without taking his Alamang.
Named after Texas A&M Research Ship "Alaminos".

Named from the city of Alaminos, in the Philippines province of Pangasinan. Established as a municipality in 1747, Alaminos is known for being the home of the famous Hundred Islands, a national park and protected area, composed of 123 islets scattered throughout the Lingayen Gulf.
Named after the Portuguese Hydrographic Survey ship Albacora (1924-1942).
In recognition of Prince Albert 1er of Monaco's work improving the knowledge of the Azores region.
Named after Francisco Albo, a navigator and member of Magellan's expedition who kept an account of the expedition.

Named in association with The Aldermen Islands, which were named by Capt. Cook in 1769 after the 'Court of Aldermen', an elected body that formed part of the City of London Corporation.

Named by John Ross in 1818, after the "Alexander", one of the vessels he commanded.

Named from the "Algerine" , a Newfoundland ship owned by Bowring Brothers of St. John's. She was chartered by the White Star Line late in the search, to operate with the Canadian government vessel "Montmagny". She left St. John's on May 15, 1912, and returned June 8, 1912. She recovered the last body, that of James McGrady, who was buried in Halifax.
Named from the nearby Alice Shoal.

Na-ed after Alix de Chazal Baissac, wife/colleague of 40-year Mauritius Fishery Officer-naturalist Jean De Baissac for whom Baissac Bank is named. For 5O years, the pair welcomed and provided significant aid to marine scientists who visited or did field work in the Mascarene region.
Named after Mike H. Allen (1948-1978), HIG researcher lost at sea when the vessel "Holoholo" was lost during an oceanographic voyage.

Named from the Almaciga tree (Agathis philippinensis), a tree native to the Philippines. Almaciga is prized for its high-grade resin, known as Manila copal. The tapping of this resin is the primary livelihood for many indigenous people in Sierra Madre mountain range and Palawan forests.
Named from the Portuguese Hydrographic survey vessel "Almeida Carvalho".

Named from the Brazilian research vessel "Almirante Câmara" that discovered this feature and conducted many surveys on the Brazilian continental Margin from 1975. Almirante Antonio Alves Câmara Junior was one of the most important persons involved in the establishment of the Brazilian Hydrographic Service.

Named from the Brazilian Navy oceanographic vessel "Almirante Câmara" that discovered this feature. The vessel name is a tribute to Admiral Antônio Alves Câmara Júnior (1891-1958), who was an important promoter of Brazilian hydrography.

Named from the blue subgiant star "Alpha Crucis", located in the South Cross constellation (Cruzeiro do Sul, in Portuguese) in the southern hemisphere, in association with the nearby Cruzeiro do Sul Rift. Alpha Crucis is the main and southern most star of the South Cross constellation and marks the bottom of the South Cross, when facing south.
Named from the research vessel "Altair" of the Russian Fisheries Ministry that worked in the area of this feature.
Named after Friedrich Althoff (1839-1909), German lawyer and patron of the 1899 Valdivia Expedition led by Carl Chun.

"Al Ghubayra" is one of the ancient names of Oman dating back to the 6th century.

"Al Jurz" is a stick and a part of Omani heritage, famous in Musandam Governorate at the North of Oman. It consists of two parts: a wooden stick and a metal axe, both being made from the local environment. The stick is decorated with geometric engravings, making it a beautiful artwork. Men in Musandam carry "Al Jurz" in traditional ceremonies.

The term "Al Kharif" refers to the unique season in the southern part of Oman that occurs during the period from June to September when the monsoon brings coolness and light rain, and turns the region into a lush green paradise, while most of the Arabian Peninsula witnesses a rise in temperature.

In 1969, R.K. Williams, the hydrographer in charge on the CCGS "John A. Macdonald", saw a shoal patch showing up suddenly on the echo sounder. He called Admiral Antony Storrs, of the Ministry of Transport, to take a look. The Admiral rushed over, saying "Where?" and then, "You mean that!" as he poked his finger at the sounder bending the stylus on the machine.
Named after the nearby Admiralteystvo Peninsula. This is the Russian spelling of "Admiralty", which was the former name of the Russian Navy.

Named in association with Admiralty Mountains on the adjacent Victoria Land in Antarctica. The mountains were discovered in 1841 by Capt. James Ross (English Royal Navy) and named by him for the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty under whose orders he served.

Named after Fyodor Prokop'yevich Afanasenkov (1912-1988), a Russian hydrographer who participated in 38 expeditions in the northern seas of the Arctic Ocean region. He participated in complex oceanographic research conducted by air expeditions in high latitudes.

Named after Afanasij Nikitin, a XVth century Russian traveller who, in 1471-1474, reached the Indian Ocean, moving from Moscow through the Volga River, Caspian and Mediterranean seas, across Persia and Buchara. He wrote a book entitled "Voyaging on the Three Seas".
Named from the South African fisheries research vessel "Africana II" which worked extensively in this area in the 1960s.

Named after Leonid Petrovich Agafonov (1914-1996), a Russian hydrographer who for more than 35 years led and personally participated in hydrographic works in the northern seas of the Novaya Zemlya, Barents and White Seas.

Named after Galina Vladimirovna Agapova (1930-2018), a marine geomorphologist and cartographer at the Russian Academy of Sciences since 1955. Named from the Agoho tree (Casuarina equisetifolia), a native Philippine tree with oval-shaped fruit. The fruits resemble cones with persistent bracts. The species can be found all over the Philippines, along sandy seashores and inland in broad sandy valleys near streams. It has been observed growing at elevations of up to 800 metres.

Named from the nearby Cape Agulhas, in South Africa, the geographic southern tip of the African continent and the beginning of the dividing line between the Atlantic and Indian Oceans.
Named from the nearby Agulhas Ridge. The feature looks like wings, hence the name.

Named in association with Aiguilles Island on the northern tip of Great Barrier Island (Aotea Island). 'Aiguilles' (the French for 'needles') describes the pointed rocks on the adjacent Needles Point.

Named from the nearby village area of Aipiri, in the northern part of Manokwari, West Papua, Indonesia.

Named from the "Bum", a traditional wooden sailing dhow that appeared in the twentieth century but the history of its use extends to ancient times and the use of the Bum ships for commercial purposes was common across the western side of the Indian Ocean and the Arabian Gulf.
"Al Ghubayra" is one of the ancient names of Oman dating back to the 6th century.

"Al Jurz" is a stick and a part of Omani heritage, famous in Musandam Governorate at the North of Oman. It consists of two parts: a wooden stick and a metal axe, both being made from the local environment. The stick is decorated with geometric engravings, making it a beautiful artwork. Men in Musandam carry "Al Jurz" in traditional ceremonies.

The term "Al Kharif" refers to the unique season in the southern part of Oman that occurs during the period from June to September when the monsoon brings coolness and light rain, and turns the region into a lush green paradise, while most of the Arabian Peninsula witnesses a rise in temperature.

Al'banov and fourteen sailors left the drifting ship near 83°N-60°E and after three months reached Cape Flora. Al'banov kept documents of the missing ship.

"Al Ghubayra" is one of the ancient names of Oman dating back to the 6th century.

It consists of two parts: a wooden stick and a metal axe, both being made from the local environment. The stick is decorated with geometric engravings, making it a beautiful artwork. Men in Musandam carry "Al Jurz" in traditional ceremonies.

The term "Al Kharif" refers to the unique season in the southern part of Oman that occurs during the period from June to September when the monsoon brings coolness and light rain, and turns the region into a lush green paradise, while most of the Arabian Peninsula witnesses a rise in temperature.

Named from the blue subgiant star "Alpha Crucis", located in the South Cross constellation (Cruzeiro do Sul, in Portuguese) in the southern hemisphere, in association with the nearby Cruzeiro do Sul Rift. Named from the first Omani ship "Sultanah" that sailed in 1840 on a historic voyage from Zanzibar to the USA. In 1969, R.K. Williams, the hydrographer in charge on the CCGS "John A. Macdonald", saw a shoal patch showing up suddenly on the echo sounder. He called Admiral Antony Storrs, of the Ministry of Transport, to take a look. The Admiral rushed over, saying "Where?" and then, "You mean that!" as he poked his finger at the sounder bending the stylus on the machine.
Named after the nearby Admiralteystvo Peninsula. This is the Russian spelling of "Admiralty", which was the former name of the Russian Navy.

Named in association with Admiralty Mountains on the adjacent Victoria Land in Antarctica. The mountains were discovered in 1841 by Capt. James Ross (English Royal Navy) and named by him for the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty under whose orders he served.

Named after Fyodor Prokop'yevich Afanasenkov (1912-1988), a Russian hydrographer who participated in 38 expeditions in the northern seas of the Arctic Ocean region. He participated in complex oceanographic research conducted by air expeditions in high latitudes.

Named after Afanasij Nikitin, a XVth century Russian traveller who, in 1471-1474, reached the Indian Ocean, moving from Moscow through the Volga River, Caspian and Mediterranean seas, across Persia and Buchara. He wrote a book entitled "Voyaging on the Three Seas".
Named from the South African fisheries research vessel "Africana II" which worked extensively in this area in the 1960s.

Named after Leonid Petrovich Agafonov (1914-1996), a Russian hydrographer who for more than 35 years led and personally participated in hydrographic works in the northern seas of the Novaya Zemlya, Barents and White Seas.

Named from the Brazilian research vessel "Almirante Câmara" that discovered this feature and conducted many surveys on the Brazilian continental Margin from 1975. Almirante Antonio Alves Câmara Junior was one of the most important persons involved in the establishment of the Brazilian Hydrographic Service.

Named from the Brazilian Navy oceanographic vessel "Almirante Câmara" that discovered this feature. The vessel name is a tribute to Admiral Antônio Alves Câmara Júnior (1891-1958), who was an important promoter of Brazilian hydrography.

Named from the blue subgiant star "Alpha Crucis", located in the South Cross constellation (Cruzeiro do Sul, in Portuguese) in the southern hemisphere, in association with the nearby Cruzeiro do Sul Rift. Alpha Crucis is the main and southern most star of the South Cross constellation and marks the bottom of the South Cross, when facing south.
Named from the research vessel "Altair" of the Russian Fisheries Ministry that worked in the area of this feature.
